chunks: And from him, from Al-Hasan ibn Ali ibn Yusuf, from Uthman ibn Isa, from Abdullah ibn Muskan, from some of our companions, who said:

I heard Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) saying: 'Indeed, the woman is a necklace, so look at what she adorns herself with.' He said, 'And I heard him saying: The woman has no danger, neither for her righteous ones nor for her wicked ones. As for her righteous ones, her danger is not gold and silver, and she is better than gold and silver. And as for her wicked ones, her danger is not dust, and dust is better than her.'

key_terms.صَالِحَتِهِنَّ: Her righteous ones (referring to the women themselves or their nature)
key_terms.طَالِحَتِهِنَّ: Her wicked ones (referring to the women themselves or their nature)
key_terms.قِلَادَةٌ: Necklace, used here as a metaphor for adornment and value

ai.seo_question: What is the metaphorical meaning of a woman being described as a 'necklace' in Shia hadith?
ai.summary: In the chapter on choosing spouses, Imam Al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) employs the metaphor of a necklace to illustrate that a woman's value is determined by her character, framing her as both a precious adornment and a potential risk. He contrasts the righteousness of a virtuous woman, whose worth surpasses gold and silver, with the danger of a wicked one, whose impact exceeds even that of dust. This hadith underscores the Shia scholarly emphasis on moral integrity as the primary criterion in marital selection, moving beyond superficial attributes to assess spiritual and practical compatibility.
